issues.issue: The execution date is left partly blank/illegible ("September _/3"), so the date the trust was made is not fixed on the face of the instrument. That is a mechanical gap rather than an ambiguity of meaning, and the parties are otherwise clearly identified.

The recited amounts do not match: the Grantor is said to pay "Seventy-five and no/100 Dollars" yet the figure is written "$375.00", and that sum is to buy a $100 face Series E Bond. The word-versus-figure discrepancy is a mechanical error a court could be asked to resolve, though it affects only a nominal corpus.

The defining clause says "two (3) certificates" and then gives both the John Hancock and the Metropolitan certificates the identical number 819800, so the identification of the res is internally erroneous. Because "Policies of Insurance" is the operative defined term for the whole trust, a mistake in its identification is capable of being construed.

The reservation of a right "to add to this trust from time to time" runs into text that survives only as "...life which, when delivered to the Trustee", so the class of addable property (apparently further policies on Grantor's life) is not clearly stated. The scope of what may later be brought under the trust is therefore uncertain on the face of the clause.

The Trustee is given absolute-owner powers to "change beneficiaries", surrender, cancel or assign the Policies, which sits awkwardly with Article XIII's irrevocability and with Article VI's fixed dispositive scheme for the proceeds. A court could be asked whether the power to change beneficiaries can be exercised so as to defeat the Article VI beneficiaries.

The clause incorporates the attached Metropolitan assignment "as fully as if set out verbatim", and that assignment contains a New York construction clause that collides with Article XI's Tennessee governing-law provision. Incorporating the whole of the assignment thus imports a choice-of-law conflict into the trust instrument.

The sentence is ungrammatical ("The Trustee may, but shall not be obliged, to pay premiums"), and the exception "except that it shall apply any dividends" is attached to a no-liability clause rather than to the permissive power. Whether the dividend-application duty is a mandatory duty or merely a limit on the exculpation is arguable.

The provision says forfeiture proceeds "shall be distributed as hereinafter directed", but Article VI directs distribution only upon the deaths of the Grantor and his wife, so it is unclear whether cash taken on forfeiture during life is distributed at once or merely held. The cross-reference "as hereinafter directed" has no self-contained timing.

The statement that the Trustee is "under no obligation or duty whatever" except safekeeping and receipt of proceeds cannot be squared with the affirmative duties imposed elsewhere — Article III's duty to apply dividends to premiums and Article VI.A's duties to invest, collect income and pay the wife quarterly. A court would have to harmonise the blanket disclaimer with those express duties.

The absolute "shall incur no liability" for estate purchases and loans conflicts with Article XII, which exculpates the Trustee "except its own bad faith or negligence". A court would have to decide whether negligent self-dealing with the estate is nonetheless excused.

The encroachment power turns on whether income is insufficient to maintain the wife "in accordance with the standard of living to which she has been accustomed during Grantor's life", taking account of "any other income" she may have. Both the standard and the duty to consider outside resources are classically contestable measures of a discretionary invasion of principal.

The clause directs division into "two (2) equal parts, one of which shall be distributed to each of Grantor's children, Mark Andrew Scott and Paul Ethan Scott, and any later children born of Grantor's marriage", which cannot work if there is a later-born child: a fixed two-way split contradicts an open class of takers. It is also unclear whether the later-born class, and the trigger "upon Grantor's death if Grantor's wife shall predecease him", fix the shares as of the Grantor's death or the wife's.

The limitation to children "born of Grantor's marriage to his wife, Sarah Oneida Covington Scott" sits against Article VI.C, which repeatedly contemplates "adopted children" as takers, leaving unclear whether adopted or later non-marital children share. Reading the two subparagraphs together produces an inconsistent description of the class of children.

Subparagraph (1) breaks off at "To his then surviving lawful issue or adopted" and, unlike (2), contains no "per stirpes" direction, so the manner of division among a deceased child's issue is not stated. The mismatch between (1) and (2) is a mechanical defect in the substitutional gift.

The default gift sends one-half to those who would inherit "the real property of such deceased child" under Tennessee intestacy, a measuring device that fits awkwardly where the fund is personalty and where more than one child may have died. The named institutions are then to use the gift "in the way and manner they see fit", which leaves no restriction to construe but does depend on the institutions still existing.

Appearing as subparagraph (4) within Article VI.C but speaking of "any portion of the trust estate passing under the terms of this instrument", the clause's reach is uncertain: it may govern only the substitutional gifts in C or every distribution under the instrument. Its placement and its general words pull in opposite directions.

Requiring the Trustee to hold a minor's share until majority is difficult to reconcile with Article VII, which permits payment for a minor beneficiary to be made "directly to such person being a minor" or to any other person for the minor's benefit. A court would have to decide which regime governs a minor's share.
